title: Patellofemoral Pain
case: Case: A 24-year-old recreational runner has 8 weeks of pain around the front of the right knee after increasing weekly distance. It is worse on stairs downward and after sitting. No swelling, locking or giving way. Squat and step-down reproduce the pain. Hip abduction strength is reduced. Hip examination is normal.

Working diagnosis: patellofemoral pain. Plan: education, reduce running volume by about half, begin isometrics, then knee and hip strengthening, add taping if it helps, graded return to running, reassess every 2 weeks.

differentials.name: Patellar tendinopathy
differentials.key: Pain at the lower pole of the patella, load-related, jumpers

differentials.name: Fat pad impingement
differentials.key: Pain beside the tendon, worse with full extension

differentials.name: Osgood-Schlatter or Sinding-Larsen-Johansson
differentials.key: Adolescent, tender bony point below or at the patella

differentials.name: Hip pathology referred to the knee (including slipped capital femoral epiphysis in adolescents)
differentials.key: Limp, limited hip rotation, groin or thigh pain
differentials.next: Urgent if suspected in an adolescent

differentials.name: Stress fracture or tumour
differentials.key: Constant or night pain, bony tenderness

qa: Why are grind and compression tests not enough? They have poor accuracy and many pain-free knees are tender or noisy, so functional tests and history are more useful [Ref - to verify].
Why do we avoid saying the kneecap is out of place? The tracking explanation is not well supported and can increase fear of movement.
A 14-year-old has knee pain and a limp. What do you check? The hip. Limited painful hip rotation needs urgent referral to exclude a slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
Why strengthen the hip as well as the knee? Consensus statements recommend combined knee and hip exercise, because it may give better pain relief than knee exercise alone [Ref - to verify].
The knee suddenly locks and will not straighten. What now? Suspect a mechanical block, refer for orthopaedic review.

fields.Purpose: Reproduce the familiar pain in a loaded, weight-bearing position and observe movement control
fields.Position: Standing on the painful leg, hands on hips or free, facing a mirror if possible
fields.Action: Slowly squat on one leg to about 45 to 60 degrees of knee bend, or step down from a low step and tap the heel lightly. Repeat several times
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the familiar anterior knee pain
fields.Supports: PFP, particularly when the double-leg squat is also painful
fields.Movement observation: Note if the trunk leans, the pelvis drops or the knee moves inward. These are observations, not proof of cause
fields.Limits: Pain only shows that the joint is irritable. Visual movement ratings vary between observers [Ref - to verify]
fields.Next step: Use the test as a baseline for monitoring treatment

fields.Position: Supine, knee bent to about 20 to 30 degrees and relaxed
fields.Positive: The patient shows apprehension, contracts the quadriceps or resists
fields.Next step: If positive, use the instability pathway and consider medical review

redFlags.Finding: Adolescent with knee pain, limp and limited or painful hip rotation
redFlags.Why it matters: Hip problem referred to the knee

redFlags.Finding: Hot, red, swollen knee with fever
Fall or injury with immediate swelling, inability to bear weight or a visible deformity
redFlags.Immediate action: Use local injury rules; refer for imaging

redFlags.Finding: Constant night pain, weight loss, a bony lump

manual.name: Soft-tissue work (quadriceps, iliotibial band region, calf)
manual.why: Short-term comfort and ease of exercise

manual.name: Patellar glides
manual.why: Short-term pain relief in some patients [Ref - to verify]
manual.finding: Stiff painful patella with limited glide
manual.application: Supine, gentle medial, lateral and superior glides

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education and exercise. Manual therapy alone is not enough. Do not claim to correct kneecap tracking or realign the patella through manual techniques. Where manual therapy is used, combine it with exercise [Ref - to verify].

exercise.Exercise: Isometric quadriceps hold (wall sit at shallow angle, or seated knee extension hold)
exercise.Steps: Hold with knee bent about 45 to 60 degrees
exercise.Regress when: Pain above 5 out of 10 or lasting into the next day

exercise.Steps: Lying on the side, lift the top leg

exercise.Exercise: Clam or banded hip external rotation

exercise.Steps: As in Vol 4 Ch 1; add load
Graded walk to run, then volume and speed

exercise.When to consider: Short-term pain relief to allow exercise
exercise.Comment: Evidence mixed; use only if it helps in the session [Ref - to verify]

exercise.When to consider: Short-term benefit in some patients, especially with flat or pronated feet

exerciseNotes: Principle: consensus statements place exercise therapy, combining knee and hip exercises, as the first-line treatment, often for at least 3 months, together with education and load management [Ref - to verify]. The aim is to increase the capacity of the knee to take load.

Symptom rule: pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 during exercise that settles within 24 hours is acceptable [Ref - to verify]. Avoid long periods of the most painful activity during the early weeks, but do not stop activity altogether.

Load management: reduce, rather than stop, painful activity. For runners, lower weekly volume or intensity, shorten the stride length slightly or raise the step rate a little (about 5 to 10 percent) in selected cases, then rebuild gradually [Ref - to verify].

modalities.name: Therapeutic ultrasound, laser, electrical stimulation as a routine treatment
modalities.comment: Weak or no added benefit [Ref - to verify]

modalityNotes: Injections and surgery are rarely needed for PFP and are medical decisions.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Adolescent with a limp or hip signs? Yes: hip examination and urgent referral if needed.
Anterior knee pain around the patella with typical triggers and a positive squat or step-down test, and no locking, major swelling or injury? Yes: working diagnosis is patellofemoral pain.
Another condition fits better (tendinopathy, instability, meniscal)? Use that pathway.
Start exercise therapy with education and load management.
If no improvement after a suitable trial, review the diagnosis and consider medical opinion.
Visit 1: screen flags and the hip (especially in adolescents), confirm the diagnosis, explain the condition and expected recovery, set goals.
Early: manage load, start isometrics and gentle strengthening, optional taping or orthoses.
